headlines.title: Valkyries fever ramps up in Bay Area ahead of WNBA Finals Game 1 at Ballhalla
headlines.description: Bay Area hoops will be in the national spotlight with the WNBA Finals tipping off Saturday at San Francisco’s Chase Center. The best-of-seven series features the Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream both competing for each respective franchise’s first title. Both teams are known for being defensive juggernauts. Golden State’s deep playoff run has united the Bay Area, with fans attending Chase Center games expected to make “Ballhalla” a nightmare for the Dream. What were the results from Valkyries vs. Dream regular season games? The Valkyries swept the regular-season series against the Dream, winning two games at home and one on the road. Golden State recorded victories of 77-66 and 78-75 over Atlanta at Ballhalla in late June before beating the Dream 88-83 in the most recent meeting July 4. Golden State Valkyries Oct 15 WNBA Oct 12 WNBA Oct 12 Postseason experience Atlanta is looking for its first title, but have made three Finals trips ahead of this year’s series against Golden State. The Valkyries made history in their inaugural season last year by qualifying for the 2025 WNBA Playoffs as the No. 8 seed with a 23–21 regular-season. Who has home-court advantage in the WNBA Finals? The Valkyries have home court due to being the higher seed. Golden State will host Games 1 and 2 at Ballhalla, along with the potential Games 5 and 7. How to watch Valkyries vs. Dream in the WNBA Finals The series will air across NBC and USA Network. Games 1 and 4 will be on NBC Bay Area. All games can also be streamed on Peacock. Where to stream Valkyries vs. Dream WNBA Finals games live online In addition to Peacock, there are other platforms where the Finals can be streamed. NBC broadcasts can also be seen on NBC.com and the NBC app, while USA Network broadcasts are available to watch on USANetwork.com and the USA Network app. Valkyries vs. Dream WNBA Finals schedule Here’s the full Finals broadcast schedule: Game 1: Dream at Valkyries — Saturday, Oct. 17, 3:30 p.m. ET/12:30 p.m. PT, NBC and Peacock Game 2: Dream at Valkyries — Monday, Oct. 19, 8 p.m. ET/5 p.m. PT, Peacock and USA Network Game 3: Valkyries at Dream — Wednesday, Oct. 21, 8 p.m. ET/5 p.m. PT, Peacock and USA Network Game 4: Valkyries at Dream — Saturday, Oct. 24, 1 p.m. ET/10 a.m. PT, NBC and Peacock Game 5 (if necessary): Dream at Valkyries — Monday, Oct. 26, 8 p.m. ET/5 p.m. PT, Peacock and USA Network Game 6 (if necessary): Valkyries at Dream — Thursday, Oct. 29, 8 p.m. ET/5 p.m. PT, Peacock and USA Network Game 7 (if necessary): Dream at Valkyries — Saturday, Oct. 31, 8 p.m. ET/5 p.m. PT, Peacock and USA Network

headlines.title: Mail-in ballots stolen from Daly City post office
headlines.description: The U.S. Postal Service is investigating after vote-by-mail ballots for San Mateo County were stolen from a Daly City post office, the county’s Registration & Elections Division said Thursday. The Elections Division said it was notified Wednesday of the mail theft that reportedly included mail-in ballots. The number of ballots that were stolen is still unknown. The county is working with USPS to investigate. Voters who are concerned that their ballots may have been affected by the theft may request a replacement ballot online or in person at any vote center in the county. Online requests for a replacement ballot must be submitted by Oct. 27 to allow sufficient time for mailing. Voters are encouraged to look up the status of their mail-in ballots through the California Secretary of State’s free ballot tracking service, “Where’s My Ballot.” The platform notifies voters when their ballot is mailed, received, and processed by the county elections division. There are currently three vote centers open in the county. Additional centers will open on Saturday, Oct. 24 and Saturday, Oct. 31, bringing the total to 50 vote centers. For a list of vote centers and ballot drop off locations, go to smcacre.gov. Voters with questions about their ballot status can contact the elections division at registrar@smcacre.gov or 650-312-5222.

headlines.title: Who is Elizabeth Holmes and what did she do?
headlines.description: Elizabeth Holmes continues to be a pop culture fascination and cautionary tale of hubris among tech start-up founders. The former CEO of the health technology company is the subject of the new documentary, “You Can See Everything,” which hits theaters on Oct. 16. The trailer for the film went viral in September for its eerie interactions between Holmes and comedian Nathan Fielder as well as its depiction of Holmes’ family life with partner Billy Evans and their two young children. The film is just the latest project involving the saga of Holmes, which has previously spawned an HBO documentary and a scripted Hulu series. Here’s what to know about her story and the new film. Movies Sep 7 Crime and Courts Sep 24 Who is Elizabeth Holmes? Holmes dropped out of Stanford University at 19 years old in 2003 to start Theranos, a Silicon Valley company that promised to revolutionize healthcare. The company’s stated goal was to use technology to run hundreds of blood tests using only a simple pinprick of blood in a proprietary machine Theranos called the Edison. Holmes raised nearly $1 billion from several prominent investors, including Oracle founder Larry Ellison, media mogul Rupert Murdoch, and heirs of the Walton family that owns Walmart. By 2014, Theranos was valued at $9 billion. She became a darling of Silicon Valley, appearing on a 2014 cover of Forbes that billed her as the world’s youngest self-made female billionaire due to her 50% stake in Theranos. In 2015, she was named one of Time Magazine’s 100 most influential people. The company’s image began to unravel after a series of investigative articles by The Wall Street Journal in 2015 raised serious questions about whether the Theranos technology worked. The saga was also detailed in the 2018 book “Bad Blood” by WSJ journalist John Carreyrou. Theranos was using existing commercially available blood-analysis technology and repurposing it to run its blood tests, according to The Wall Street Journal. A former Theranos lab associate who became a whistleblower testified at Holmes’ trial that the Edison machines routinely failed quality control tests and that their results were about as accurate as “flipping a coin,” according to CNBC. An investigation into the company resulted in the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing civil fraud charges against Theranos, Holmes and former president Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani. What did Elizabeth Holmes get convicted of? In January 2022, Holmes was convicted by a jury in a California court of four federal charges of wire fraud for misrepresenting to investors what the Theranos technology could do and how widely its Edison machines were being adopted. Prosecutors alleged that she duped investors into pouring money into a product she knew was faulty. Holmes denied the accusation during the trial. “At the time, you were not worried people would be given an inaccurate impression?” Assistant U.S. Attorney Robert Leach asked her during the trial. “I was not,” Holmes said. Holmes was acquitted of charges of defrauding patients and one count of conspiracy. In May 2023, U.S. District Judge Edward Davila ordered her to pay $452 million in restitution to the victims of her crimes. Is Elizabeth Holmes still in prison? Yes, Holmes was sentenced to 11 years and 3 months in federal prison in November 2022. Balwani was sentenced to nearly 13 years in prison and three years of probation after being convicted of 12 counts of fraud. Holmes, 42, has been serving her sentence at a minimum-security prison in Bryan, Texas, but she is expected to be let out of prison into a halfway house. She is scheduled to be transferred to a halfway house next year, according to one of her victims. Alan Eisenman, who invested about $1.2 million in Theranos, told NBC News on Sept. 24 that he was notified that she is to be transferred to the Austin Transitional Center in an unincorporated community that borders Austin, Texas. The Department of Justice is required by law to notify victims of crime of case developments through letters and emails. Her scheduled release date is Feb. 22, 2030, after some reductions in her sentence. What makes the new movie different from previous projects? “You Can See Everything” is the latest film involving Holmes, and the most intimate. Amanda Seyfried won an Emmy for outstanding lead actress for her portrayal of Holmes in the 2022 scripted series “The Dropout” on Hulu. Holmes was also the subject of the 2019 HBO documentary “The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley.” In “You Can See Everything,” Holmes grants comedian Nathan Fielder and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim extraordinary access to her life in the months leading up to when she entered prison. She had a son with partner Billy Evans in 2021 and then gave birth to a daughter in 2023, shortly before she began serving her prison sentence. The documentary trailer shows Holmes maintaining that she did nothing wrong and reveals that Fielder moved into her home while filming. “I think this is the moment in time to capture this story before I’m gone,” she seemingly tells the comedian at one point. Evans also appears in the documentary and answers questions about his life with Holmes. There are also uncomfortable moments between Fielder and Holmes, including one in which he muses about whether he can trust her. “That’s because I don’t have anything to hide,” she tells him. This story first appeared on TODAY.com. More from TODAY: Hilary Swank, 52, Addresses Backlash Over Having a Baby Later in Life Baby Name Consultant Shares 1 Classic Baby Girl Name Nobody is Using — But Should What to Know About ‘Breaking Bad’ Actor RJ Mitte’s Cause of Death and Cerebral Palsy Diagnosis

headlines.title: Driver says he was asleep when Tesla crashed into CHP patrol car on I-80
headlines.description: Two California Highway Patrol officers are recovering after a Tesla hit one of their parked patrol cars on Interstate 80 in Fairfield earlier this week. CHP posted video online showing the crash, which happened Tuesday night west of Air Base Parkway. The officers were responding to a deadly crash when the Tesla drove through the crash site and hit the parked patrol car. The driver claimed he was asleep while using driver-assistance technology. It is unknown whether the Tesla’s Full Self-Driving feature was active at the time of the collision.

headlines.title: Authorities remove 44 dogs from Vallejo woman with previous animal cruelty conviction
headlines.description: Solano County sheriff’s deputies and animal control officers on Thursday removed 44 dogs from the home of a Vallejo woman who has previously been convicted of animal cruelty. The raid, authorized by a search warrant as part of an animal cruelty investigation into resident Susan Anthony, took place at a residence on the 800 block of Carolina Street in central Vallejo. “It’s a lot of dogs, so it’s overwhelming the shelter system,” said Sgt. Rex Hawkins from the Solano County Sheriff’s Office. “Dogs are being taken everywhere.” Hawkins did not comment on the health of the canines or the conditions they were living in, but said that a veterinary assessment of the canines is pending. Anthony runs California Carolina Dogs, a dog breeding and adoption business. She has kept and bred Carolina dogs, also known as American dingos, at several Vallejo properties for around 20 years, she said. Since 2013, neighbors and animal rights groups have lodged complaints against Anthony for operating a “puppy mill.” In May, Anthony was found guilty in Solano County Court on one count of animal cruelty for allegedly keeping and breeding a pack of dogs that ran wild on a small ranch in east Vallejo. According to court records, she was granted probation in June. On August 2023, a dog owned by Anthony was attacked so badly it had to be euthanized. In 2024, a puppy was killed by several dogs, and in one week, the pack twice attacked two of Anthony’s other dogs. Anthony is also in the midst of a civil suit brought by Caru Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals alleging that her organization’s practices are animal cruelty. She is scheduled to appear in court for a hearing in the case on Friday at Solano County Superior Court in Fairfield. Anthony, who was present during Thursday’s raid, maintained that the dogs are healthy and live a good life on the property, which sits on two lots in a residential area of Vallejo. Anthony said the raid was traumatic for the dogs, some of which yelped as they were caught and put into kennels. She said the dogs belong to her 99-year-old mother, who lives on Carolina Street. Anthony has vigorously defended her dog operation. In September 2025, she filed a motion for a restraining order against the county Animal Control, which was denied.

headlines.title: Natalie Nakase's high-energy, hands-on coaching has guided Golden State Valkyries to WNBA Finals
headlines.description: Natalie Nakase throws her arms up to guard Gabby Williams one moment, then moves to defend Veronica Burton the next as Golden State’s high-octane coach gets into it to help the Valkyries gear up for the WNBA Finals. She briefly steps out of the action to observe before jumping right back in to take a turn against Tiffany Hayes. And you bet Nakase can trash talk with the best of them. “Oh, yeah, I say, ‘Yeahhh!’ I say, ‘Not here! Not this time!,” she shared Wednesday. “I let them know. Because that’s effort. Again, it goes back to you can control that. I’m 46 years old, why am I getting that (stop)?” Nakase never stops moving, and it’s why everyone around her is offering regular reminders that she needs to eat for energy and rest just the way she stresses those things to her players. The coach collapsed on the court late in the deciding game of the first round with Dallas and later called it “a wakeup call” to prioritize her well being. Her players love and appreciate how hands-on she is with practices and game planning. “It probably brings back some memories of her being in uniform when she used to play,” Hayes said. “It’s definitely fun, but it’s more fun when we actually get the bucket on it ‘cause if she gets the stop we won’t hear the end of it.” That intensity and drive is something Hayes has seen for years, dating to their days when Nakase was an assistant with the Las Vegas Aces coaching Hayes and the guards. And it played a key role in Hayes following her to the Bay Area. Nakase had just been hired for her first head coaching job when she asked Hayes to take a chance on a brand new team and join her in San Francisco and start something special with the expansion Valkyries. Hayes had absolutely no reservations and the answer was a resounding yes. Her unfamiliarity with the Bay Area hardly mattered, because she had Nakase –- and that’s a sentiment many of Golden State’s players feel given how much she has invested in each one of them. Nakase has built a culture with the Valkyries in such a short time largely by finding a way to know each woman on a deeper level, far beyond just basketball. WNBA 3 hours ago WNBA Oct 12 She is breaking barriers With the Valkyries and their famous, violet-colored “Ballhalla” fan base on the big postseason stage, everybody is getting a glimpse of what Nakase vowed to do from Day 1: put Golden State on the map for women’s basketball after all those special NBA championship runs by Stephen Curry, Steve Kerr and the Warriors. And, no, she’s not surprised by the playoff success so soon — she thought the Valkyries should have made a run last year, when they lost in the first round to Minnesota after becoming the first expansion franchise to reach the postseason in its inaugural year. Nakase was groomed by some greats: Clippers coach Tyronn Lue, former Los Angeles assistant Armond Hill, who has been attending practice in Oakland this week, and Aces coach Becky Hammon. “You just celebrate people that are blowing away ceilings for women in sports, specifically women’s basketball, and obviously we’re a little biased toward Natalie,” UCLA coach Cori Close said of Nakase, the former Bruins guard. “I just think about what she’s done. She came to UCLA as a walk-on, then earned a scholarship, then became a captain, then was one of the first women hired on an NBA team and 10 years with the Clippers and really doing a great job with Becky Hammon and winning championships there. And now coming here and they say, ‘We want to win it in the first five years,’ and she’s like, ‘Bring it on, that’s exactly the kind of organization I want to be a part of,’ and then go back it up and then sell out every game. The list just goes on and on.” Nakase has found a way to relate to all of her players, and she works at it. Whether it’s learning about their culture or language, favorite music or dance move, she makes an effort to know everyone on her team far beyond just basketball. “I think my identity changes from year to year because I’m a constant learner,” she said. Uplifting the group does wonders Celebrating in the locker room after winning on Las Vegas’ home floor last Friday, Nakase praised her team for its fight in overtime to eliminate the defending champion Aces. She pointed to Kiah Stokes for making a key block, and teammates broke into chants of “Ki-ah! Ki-ah!” Then it was Kayla Thornton’s turn to be shouted out, for her rebounding. And cheers of “K-T, K-T!” The coach finished by acknowledging her two clutch finishers in crunch time, “the closers, you two,” and pointed at Hayes and Williams. Players started hollering “Tip! Tip! Tip!” and “Gab-by! Gab-by!” The Valkyries rallied from an 11-point deficit to pull off an 87-77 overtime victory in Las Vegas for an improbable sweep in the best-of-five WNBA semifinals. “Down 11 meant nothing, right? You guys stayed connected, you guys stayed composed. What I loved was your fight, everyone brought another level of fight,” Nakase told them. “It was pure joy.” Success has affected her health But this special season hasn’t come without challenges for Nakase. She scared her family and everybody else when she went down in the closing minutes of the clinching Game 3 against the Wings earlier this month. Yet the coach got back up and finished the final 1:40. When Nakase saw her sister in tears afterward, she realized she had to take better care of herself to be there for others. She leaned more on her assistants. “You could want to win as much as you want but if my tank is not full, whether it’s rest, food, hydration, everything, then I’m not going to be able to give my full self during the game as you guys saw,” she said. “It’s doing that.” Nakase’s late father, Gary, influenced most everything she does. She watched him overdo it at times. Her former players are accustomed to how hard Nakase pushes herself. “That’s Natalie and that’s about giving her all, literally 100%,” Aces center A’ja Wilson said. “She’s a warrior, it’s what she does. She eats, sleeps, breathes basketball.” Valkyries owner Joe Lacob could see it when he interviewed Nakase over a late breakfast in Las Vegas two years ago. “She’s everything I thought she would be,” Lacob said. “I’m so happy for her, she continues to impress me with her coaching, she’s just terrific.” While handling video duties as an intern for the Clippers, Hill asked what her goal was and Nakase told him she wanted to be a head coach one day. He replied, “OK, let’s get to it.” “He’s the reason why I’m here, seriously,” she said. “… He calls me grasshopper, because I’m always anxious, I want to do everything right, I’m a perfectionist, I’m an extremist but he’s all about, ‘Hey, just take a breath, make sure you’re clear and concise with your game plan, try not to get everything done all in one night and more importantly take care of your health.’” She honors her late father every day in all she does, committed to treating the job as a tremendous opportunity. “I’m always going to be a fighter,” Nakase said. “That’s how my dad raised me.” ___ See AP’s full WNBA coverage here

headlines.title: PG&E says power could be restored early for thousands in Bay Area
headlines.description: Thousands of people in the Bay Area are entering their second day without power, but the outage could end earlier than originally planned. PG&E has indicated that people in parts of the East Bay could have power restored around 4 p.m. Friday instead of around 2 p.m. Saturday as originally planned. Customers in the North Bay could have power restored around 7 p.m. Friday. PG&E’s outage website shows areas without power due to high fire risk, including parts of Contra Costa, Alameda, Sonoma and Napa counties. The utility shut off power to nearly 80,000 customers statewide, including around 6,200 in the East Bay, in what PG&E says is the largest Public Safety Power Shutoff since 2020. PG&E said it shut off the power to prevent power lines from sparking a wildfire amid hot, dry conditions that were expected to be windy. Some people without power have questioned PG&E’s decision because it hasn’t been windy in some locations. NBC Bay Area’s Bob Redell has the full report in the video above. East Bay 14 hours ago PG&E Oct 15 Bay Area Oct 14 PG&E Oct 13 PG&E warns Bay Area customers of possible shutoffs amid high winds, dry conditions

headlines.title: Man arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after San Jose stabbing
headlines.description: Police in San Jose arrested a man who allegedly approached and stabbed a stranger in September, the department said Thursday. On Sept. 26, officers were sent to a San Jose hospital after receiving a report of a man with stab wounds. The victim told police he had been walking in the area of Branham Lane and Kingspark Drive when a man unknown to him approached him; the suspect grabbed the man and stabbed him multiple times before leaving the scene. The victim was able to take himself to the hospital and survived. Surveillance footage was obtained and detectives identified the suspect as Paul Marquez, 30. An arrest warrant was issued for Marquez and he was apprehended on Oct. 3 in San Jose. Marquez was booked into jail on suspicion of attempted murder and assault with a deadly weapon. Due to the random nature of the alleged attack, detectives are concerned there may be more victims. Anyone with information about this case or similar cases is asked to contact Detective Wilson via email at 4917@sanjoseca.gov or by phone at 408-277-4161.

headlines.title: 2 arrested for allegedly pulling gun on father, assaulting mother at San Jose restaurant
headlines.description: Two people were arrested on suspicion of assaulting two parents with their child at a fast food restaurant in San Jose in August, police said Thursday. On Aug. 3 just before 9 p.m., a man and a woman with their young daughter were in a fast food restaurant in the 1100 block of South King Road in San Jose when a woman physically assaulted the mother after an altercation. The father attempted to intervene and the male suspect began to assault him, according to police. The male then brandished a gun at the father and threatened to shoot him. The suspects fled the scene before police could arrive. Detectives used license plate readers to identify a vehicle allegedly associated with the suspects and arrested Alejandro Valencia, 30, and Krystelle Tieu Acosta, 23, in Union City on Oct. 7. A search warrant was issued for their residence and police allegedly found two guns and evidence linking them to the crime. Both were booked into jail on suspicion of assault with a deadly weapon, felony battery and making criminal threats.

headlines.title: CTE study on NFL players raises questions about California's youth concussion protocol
headlines.description: There is renewed concern about whether enough is being done to prevent youth sports concussions following a major study that found at least a quarter of NFL players are expected to develop a degenerative brain disease. “What’s happening when these individuals are younger? How many little hits are they getting that leads to them having CTE,” asked Dr. Nirav Pandya, a pediatric orthopedic surgeon with UCSF Benioff who specializes in sports medicine for young athletes. “And what can we do at that younger age group to prevent these athletes from getting that?” Concussions in general affect around two million teenagers and children in the U.S. every year, according to the National Center for Health Statistics. Boys tackle football has the highest rate of concussions, according to the CDC, and girls soccer is number two. Girls have a higher change of sports-related concussions than boys, the agency said, in part because girls may report more and health care professionals like athletic trainers are less likely to be at girls’ practices and games to identify injuries. California’s student athlete concussion protocol In California, school coaches are required to take an online training course on concussions. If they suspect a concussion, they must remove the student athlete from the game or practice for at least that day until cleared by a licensed health care provider. If a concussion is confirmed, the student must complete a gradual return-to-play protocol lasting at least seven days. California’s student athlete concussion protocol. “I think the tough thing with all of this is that you are basing it on a kid reporting symptoms and someone identifying them,” said Dr. Pandya. He said he recently had a patient whose concussions went undiagnosed for over a year. “He had horrible headaches, had problems learning for over a year and had multiple concussions and hadn’t gotten treatment,” Dr. Pandya said. “A concussion, there’s no MRI; no blood test for it.” Reporter Candice Nguyen (left) and Dr. Nirav Pandya (right). Ben Nguyen’s concussion story Earlier this year, Ben Nguyen, a senior at Archbishop Mitty High School in San Jose, California, says he suffered a serious concussion during a wrestling match. “I felt incredibly nauseous,” he recalled. Nguyen shared cell phone video of the moment he got concussed. It shows his opponent go in for a takedown when Nguyen responds by trying to flip the other student over his own body. Image from video shared by Ben Nguyen. “His should and neck were kind of in my chin area,” he said. “The impact kind of went straight to my head.” The impact wasn’t obvious, but the symptoms afterward were. “I couldn’t think as fast anymore…I was like throwing up in the bus ride. I was throwing up right after my match as well,” Nguyen said. Nguyen said he felt a little nervous about telling his coach and athletic trainer, who’s a sports health care professional on the team. Ben Nguyen, Archbishop Mitty High School wrestler. “The impact looked so subtle. I was kind of scared of them being like, ‘Oh, there’s nothing, you can go back,’” Nguyen said. He said that didn’t happen and his school took his injury seriously. However, he admits, it’s easy for students to get around the concussion protocol if they want to. “I have a friend in football who had all the hallmark symptoms of concussions, he just lied on the survey to get back into practice,” he said. NBC Bay Area reached out to Archbishop Mitty High School. The school declined to participate in this story. The California Interscholastic Federation, which established the state’s student athlete concussion protocol, said it’s important for everyone involved to make sure the return-to-play process is followed. The solutions, the science, and the debate “If we can empower kids to understand that it’s okay to speak up. Number two, the system, athletic trainers, physical therapists, anyone who’s looking over these kids.Then, I think there are more drastic things that we talk about like, how can we decrease the number of chances or times that someone can get hit? Maybe that means delaying when kids start playing tackle football,” Dr. Pandya said. It’s some of those drastic suggestions that continue to be challenged. “My big concern is when we hear results about people who play the most elite level, that there’s a reaction of looking at, well, what do we do at the youth level? And these are very different games,” said David Camarillo who is Associate Professor of Bioengineering, (by courtesy) Mechanical Engineering and Neurosurgery at Stanford University. Camarillo has been studying concussions for the past 15 years testing thousands of helmets in his lab, CamLab, in Stanford. David Camarillo, Assoc. Professor of Bioengineering at Stanford University. The results he’s talking about come from a recent study published in the British Medical Journal showing at least a quarter of NFL players will likely develop a neurodegenerative disease like CTE. The NFL said it’s aware of the study, and it’s ensuring its community has access to expanding resources. Camarillo believes the science points to urgent action needed at the professional level. “Does it mean kids shouldn’t play sports? I don’t think we have enough information to say yes to that,” Camarillo said. When asked what’s the harm in taking preventative action in case certain youth sports are connected to developing CTE later in life, Camarillo said he believes taking action at an individual level is perfectly fair. “I think it’s a very different thing to make a law, to make public policy that affects everybody, that takes away a right to choose. That ought to have scientific evidence behind it,” he added. CamLab at Stanford University. Why isn’t there evidence? The British Medical Journal study relied on hundreds of NFL players donating their brains to science after they die. We don’t have that kind of data on our young athletes today. The Investigative Unit spoke to numerous doctors, researchers, and students about this issue over the past several weeks. All said the best solution right now is education, proper staffing for oversight, and schools fostering a culture where students feel encouraged to report concussion symptoms. “If it wasn’t for like my prior knowledge or like my friends or like me witnessing it first-hand, I probably would have lied to get back into wrestling,” Nguyen said. Candice Nguyen is the senior investigative reporter on this story. If you have a question about this story or a story tip, email her at candice.nguyen@nbcuni.com.

headlines.title: Lanes of Highway 101 at Hospital Curve in San Francisco to close this weekend
headlines.description: All southbound lanes and one northbound lane of Highway 101 at Hospital Curve in San Francisco will be closed this weekend for an ongoing construction project. The closure between Cesar Chavez Street and 17th Street will start at 11 p.m. Friday and continue until 6 a.m. Monday, according to Caltrans. Motorists should avoid the area and consider taking Interstate 280 as an alternate, Caltrans said. The closure will affect drivers heading out of San Francisco on the Central Freeway and those driving into San Francisco from the East Bay over the Bay Bridge, hoping through the city on highway 101. It will also affect those heading to Chase Center for the Game 1 of the WNBA Finals. This marks the third closure for the ongoing Hospital Curve repaving and rehabilitation project, which started last fall. The fourth and final closure – impacting the same lanes as this weekend’s closure – is scheduled for the weekend of Nov. 6-9, weather permitting, according to Caltrans.

headlines.title: L.A. County prosecutors weigh charges in Eric Swalwell case after sheriff's investigation
headlines.description: The Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office sex crimes unit is weighing whether to bring charges in a case involving former Rep. Eric Swalwell, a spokesperson told NBC News on Thursday. The county sheriff’s victims’ unit investigated the case, which was then forwarded to prosecutors on Sept. 21, according to the spokesperson. Swalwell, a Democrat, resigned from Congress in April and dropped out of the California governor’s race after multiple sexual assault and misconduct allegations, which he denies. Former model and fashion software company owner Lonna Drewes held a news conference in April with her attorneys in Los Angeles, accusing Swalwell of drugging, sexually assaulting and choking her. Los Angeles authorities confirmed at the time that they had launched a criminal investigation into the allegations. An attorney for Swalwell said in an email Thursday that he is “innocent,” adding that “these allegations are false, and the facts will bear that out.” “The reported referral to the Los Angeles County District Attorney is a standard procedural step. It is not a charging decision. It is not a finding of wrongdoing. It changes nothing about the facts,” said the attorney, Sara Azari. “We welcome a fair, independent review, and we are confident it will vindicate him.” The FBI searched Swalwell’s Washington, D.C., home in August and seized an electronic device in connection with an investigation that was described as involving sexual misconduct allegations at the time, according to an official familiar with the matter. The same month, FBI agents executing a search warrant stopped Swalwell at the San Francisco airport and took his electronic devices. A copy of the search warrant obtained by NBC News detailed that investigators seized an iPhone and a MacBook Pro computer. The allegations first came to light in a San Francisco Chronicle article in which a former Swalwell aide said he had sexually assaulted her twice. A source familiar with the woman’s account confirmed to NBC News that the Chronicle’s reporting was accurate. The article was followed by a CNN report in which four women, including one whose story matched the Chronicle article, made sexual misconduct allegations against him. One of the three others, Ally Sammarco, said Swalwell sent her unsolicited photos of his penis; Sammarco later spoke to NBC News and confirmed the accuracy of her account in the CNN article. Swalwell denied the accusations published by the Chronicle and CNN in a video on social media on April 10, saying, “These allegations of sexual assault are flat false.” “They did not happen. They have never happened. And I will fight them with everything I have,” he said. Swalwell served in Congress for 13 years. A special election was held in June to fill the seat he vacated upon resignation; Democrat Aisha Wahab won the race to fill out the rest of his term. The election in November for a full two-year term will be a rematch between Wahab and fellow Democrat Melissa Hernandez.
headlines.source: Andrew Blankstein and Raquel Coronell Uribe l NBC News
